title: Freight Calls, Negotiating With Voices
description: An inbound voice agent for freight brokerages: carriers call in, the system vets them, searches loads, negotiates rates, and books. Real-time voice UX, tool calling under latency constraints, and the ethics of autonomous pricing.

sections.title: The phone rings at two AM

lines.text: Two AM. A carrier calls a freight brokerage looking for a load. Nobody is in the office.
But the phone answers. A voice agent vets the carrier, searches loads, quotes a rate, negotiates, and books.
All without a human picking up.
That is the assignment. The hard part is doing all of that inside the latency budget of a phone call.
The carrier hears a professional voice asking for their MC number.
And if the carrier asks something unexpected?
The agent either handles it from its prompt or transfers to a human. The demo needs to show both paths.
This episode covers an inbound freight voice agent.
A carrier calls. The system identifies them, checks authority and insurance, matches loads, and agrees on price.
Good means natural conversation, tools fast enough to avoid silence, and correct bookings.
Define correct. Best margin or any booked load?
Both matter. But the rubric scores technical depth and customer thinking, not revenue optimization.
So the demo shows clean vetting, realistic search, and one counter-offer handled gracefully.
The platform handles speech-to-text and text-to-speech. Your job is the conversation logic and tool integrations.
So you are building a brain that sits between ears and mouth.
Exactly. The voice layer is plumbing. The intelligence is in vetting, matching, and negotiation.
Phone conversations have a latency budget. Humans notice silence after roughly seven hundred milliseconds.
Every tool call eats into it. Carrier lookup, load search, rate calculation each add round trips.
Design principle: prefetch what you can. As soon as the carrier says their MC number, start vetting before the sentence finishes.
Tool calling uses function schemas the platform exposes to the voice model. Each tool returns structured JSON.
What about interruptions? Carriers talk over the agent.
Good platforms handle barge-in natively. The harder case is partial information.
Carrier says my MC is two one four and pauses. Agent should ask for the rest rather than guessing.
Let me go deeper on latency management because it shapes every design choice.
Total budget: seven hundred milliseconds from end of caller speech to start of agent reply.
Speech recognition finalization: one hundred milliseconds. LLM inference for response generation: two hundred milliseconds.
Tool call execution: varies. FMCSA lookup five hundred milliseconds, database query under fifty. Text-to-speech synthesis: two hundred milliseconds.
Those add up to more than seven hundred already.
Yes, if sequential. Prefetching overlaps them. Start FMCSA lookup while caller is still saying their name.
Start TTS on partial results rather than waiting for complete tool response.
Function schemas define tool names, parameters with types and descriptions, and return types.
The voice model sees these schemas and decides when to invoke which tool based on conversation context.
Caller states MC number. System calls FMCSA lookup tool and gets authority status, insurance, and safety rating.
Inactive authority ends politely with callback option. Active proceeds.
Agent asks origin, destination, equipment type. Load search queries the database with those parameters.
Results include load ID, rate, weight, pickup window. Agent offers top result at asking price.
Carrier counters ten percent lower. Negotiation prompt gives floor price and maximum concession.
Agent accepts, counters once, or escalates to human.
Who sets the floor? In production, a pricing engine. In the demo, a static field per load.
The point is showing the constraint exists, not solving pricing.
Walk through a full successful call step by step.
Caller says: hi, looking for a load from Chicago to Dallas, dry van.
Agent responds: happy to help. Can I get your MC number?
Caller provides MC two-one-four-five-six-seven. Agent immediately fires FMCSA lookup while acknowledging receipt.
Lookup returns active authority, valid insurance, satisfactory safety rating.
Agent confirms carrier identity, then queries load database for Chicago-Dallas dry van loads.
Three matching loads return. Agent picks highest-paying within pickup window.
Quotes rate: twenty-three hundred dollars, picking up Thursday morning.
Carrier says twenty-one hundred or I walk.
Negotiation logic has a floor of twenty-two hundred. Agent counters at twenty-two fifty, explaining fuel cost increase.
Carrier accepts. Booking tool creates load assignment with agreed rate. Confirmation email fires automatically.
Voice synthesis adds roughly two hundred milliseconds. Speech recognition adds another hundred.
FMCSA lookup takes five hundred milliseconds. Load search should be under fifty.
Target total response: under one second from end of caller speech to agent reply start.
Cost per minute runs ten to twenty cents. A ten-minute call costs one to two dollars.
If it books a load worth two thousand dollars gross margin, negligible. Failed calls burning two dollars need monitoring.
Cost breakdown per call.
Voice platform charges roughly fifteen cents per minute including STT and TTS.
LLM inference for conversation turns adds maybe three cents per call depending on model choice.
FMCSA lookup is free government API but rate-limited. Cache results for repeat callers.
Load search against your own PostgreSQL: negligible compute cost.
Ten-minute successful booking costs about one dollar eighty total. Compare to human dispatcher salary divided by calls handled.
What about failed calls where no booking happens?
Still cost a dollar eighty. At scale, tracking conversion rate matters more than per-call cost.
Full loop again.
Call arrives. Agent greets, collects MC number, starts vetting prefetch. Authority validates. Load matches lane and equipment.
Rate quoted. Counter received. Floor logic applied: accept, counter, or escalate.
On agreement, booking tool creates record. Confirmation email fires. Call ends professionally.
Full loop once more cleanly.
Inbound call arrives. Agent greets and collects MC number. FMCSA lookup starts prefetch during collection.
Authority validates. Agent asks lane preferences. Load search matches equipment and route.
Rate quoted from top result. Negotiation applies floor logic. Agreement triggers booking and email.
Every turn logs transcript, tool invocations, and outcomes for later analysis.
Noisy truck cab degrades speech recognition. Signal: repeated clarification requests. Fix: keypad fallback for MC input.
FMCSA API times out mid-call. Signal: long silence after MC collection. Fix: timeout with hold message and retry.
Carrier lies about equipment type. Load does not fit at dock. Signal: post-booking complaint. Fix: require DOT inspection timestamp.
Pending: what are the legal constraints on automated rate agreements? Does verbal contract via AI count? Who owns negotiation logs when disputes arise?
More failure modes specific to voice.
Background engine noise causes speech recognition to hallucinate words that were never spoken.
Signal: nonsensical MC numbers or city names. Fix: confidence threshold on STT output, fallback to confirmation question.
Caller has heavy accent the model struggles with.
Signal: repeated requests to repeat. Fix: offer keypad input option after second failed attempt.
Two carriers call simultaneously and the system routes them to overlapping loads before either books.
Signal: double-booking error at dispatch. Fix: atomic reservation with short lock during booking transaction.
Pending questions: does the brokerage need consent recording notifications by state? What happens when FMCSA is down for maintenance? Who arbitrates when a carrier disputes what the AI said?
Three tests.
Can your voice agent recover from a tool timeout without dead air?
Does it escalate at the right threshold rather than making a bad deal?
Can you replay a call transcript and trace every decision to a specific tool response?
Fourth: can you replay any call and see exactly which tools fired, what they returned, and how the agent used those results?
That audit trail is what separates a demo from a deployable system.
Fifth: does the agent know what it does not know? If asked about detention fees it has no data for, does it say so or make up an answer?
Self-test: the carrier asks for a lane you have no loads on. What exactly does the agent say?
Next time: multi-turn assessment recommendation where statelessness forces better design.
What about outbound calls? Proactively calling carriers about available loads?
Different consent model, different regulatory environment. Worth exploring separately.
